p: VanderKam's Ge'ez says "wheat stew." Charles corrected it to "red," as Genesis has. Goes with 24:6.

readings.w: Charles 1902's correction: Greek pyrrou "red" (Genesis 25:30), misread as pyrou "of wheat"
VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989)

why: The Plain English Translation departs from VanderKam's Ge'ez here. Esau is named Edom ("red") because of the stew (24:6; Genesis 25:30), so "wheat" makes the explanation pointless, and the stew is made of lentils (24:3). Charles explains the slip: the Ge'ez sərnay "wheat" renders the Greek pyrou, "of wheat," which is a miscopying of pyrrou, "red." The reader can switch to VanderKam's reading.
b: Both 24:3 and 24:6 have the same word in VanderKam's text, so the same correction is made in both verses.

p: The Ge'ez says "if he makes himself strong." The Latin says "wherever he flees."

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez. Charles thought the difference "seems to have originated in the Hebrew." The Latin fits the picture of flight in Amos 9:1–4, but both readings make sense.

t: Spirit of righteousness, or Holy Spirit?
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez and most of Charles's manuscripts have "spirit of righteousness"; manuscript c has "Holy Spirit."

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's manuscripts a, b, d
Charles's manuscript c, as cited in Charles 1902

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam and the majority of manuscripts. Charles notes that the Ge'ez ṣədq can mean "righteousness" or "truth," so the phrase may stand for the Greek "spirit of truth" (compare John 14:17). He adds that "Holy Spirit" is also a Jewish expression (Isaiah 63:10–11), so manuscript c need not be a Christian change.

a: Your God put it in my way
t: "Put it in my way" or "directed me"?
p: The Ge'ez says "your God made me find it." The Latin has "the Lord your God directed me."

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez. Charles reports that his manuscript a reads "helped me" and d "caused me to see." He first emended to "directed," from the Latin, but allowed that the reading of b and c "may be right." Genesis 27:20 has "the LORD your God made it come my way."

p: VanderKam's Ge'ez has "he hid." Charles marked the words as an addition and read "that" instead.

Charles 1902's reading

why: The Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam's Ge'ez. Charles put daggers around "he hid himself and" and wrote that it "looks like an addition to the text," proposing "that" in its place, as in Genesis 27:30, where Esau comes in just as Jacob goes out.

p: The Ge'ez manuscripts differ here, and Syncellus's Greek has "when you take down" the yoke.

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam and manuscript b. Charles thought "refuse" a corruption of "become great." The Greek quoted by Syncellus, "when you take down," matches the Septuagint's rendering of Genesis 27:40 as Charles reports it, while "become great" fits the Samaritan text he cites. The difference shows how early readers struggled with the Hebrew verb in Genesis 27:40.

p: The Latin, as Charles reports it, adds "at his head," as in Genesis 28:11.

p: The Ge'ez says Jacob "slept a sleep." Charles corrected it to "woke from his sleep," as Genesis 28:16 has.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989)
Charles 1902's correction (Greek exypnōse ex hypnou, as he reconstructs it)

why: The Plain English Translation keeps VanderKam's Ge'ez, "Jacob slept a sleep," a Ge'ez way of saying he slept. It is probably a slip in the base text: as it stands, Jacob speaks at once, and 27:26 has him get up in the morning. Charles thought the manuscripts "corrupt": the Greek "he awoke from sleep" had been miscopied as "he slept a sleep." His correction matches Genesis 28:16, "Jacob woke from his sleep," and makes better sense of "and he said."

p: VanderKam's Ge'ez says Leah "too was jealous of Rachel." The Latin has only "and she gave."

The Latin lacks the jealousy, and Genesis 30:9 says only that Leah "took Zilpah her slave woman and gave her to Jacob." So Leah's jealousy rests on the Ge'ez alone.

t: "Land of Raphael" or "land of the Rephaim"?
p: VanderKam's Ge'ez first has "land of Rafael," then "land of the Rephaim." Charles reads "Rephaim" both times.

readings.w: Charles 1902 (his note gives the Ge'ez Rafâ'êm)
VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); so also Dillmann 1859, as read in the Source Library

why: The Plain English Translation departs from VanderKam's Ge'ez here. The verse explains an old name of Gilead by the people who lived there: "for it is the land of the Rephaim" (rafaʾem), and the Rephaim are named again in the next sentence. A name ending in -ʾel breaks that explanation, so it is most likely a slip of -ʾel for -ʾem, two endings that differ by one letter. Dillmann's 1859 edition has the -ʾel form at this place as well, so the slip is older than the transcription used here. Charles translates "Rephaim" both times.

t: Whom did Shechem ask: her father or his own?

Charles followed a and b, "his father," which fits Genesis 34:4, where Shechem asks his father Hamor to get Dinah for him. With "her father" Shechem goes straight to Jacob, as in Genesis 34:11, where he speaks to "her father and her brothers."

p: VanderKam's Ge'ez says they "melted" the foreign gods. Charles corrected it to "handed over," as Genesis 35:4 has.

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989); Charles's manuscript b
Charles 1902's correction (Ge'ez matawwomu)

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's Ge'ez. Charles corrected masawwomu "they melted" to matawwomu "they handed over," because Genesis 35:4 says "They handed Jacob all the foreign gods" and because Rachel then "gave" the idols to Jacob. Melting down idols and ornaments is also a known practice (Exodus 32:20), so the Ge'ez reading makes sense as it stands.

why: The Plain English Translation follows VanderKam's Ge'ez. Charles found the Ge'ez manuscripts divided and judged the Latin "decidedly better," since a priest's task is to know and teach God's ways (31:15). He offered two ways to restore the line, so the exact older wording is uncertain.

p: The Ge'ez says "make them great." The Latin says "will make them holy."

p: The Ge'ez has three titles. The Latin, as Charles reports it, omits the third, "and chiefs."

readings.w: VanderKam's Ge'ez text (1989)
readings.en: and rulers and princes and chiefs

readings.w: The Latin version (Milan palimpsest, 5th-6th century), as cited in Charles 1902

why: The Plain English Translation follows the Ge'ez. The third word, mälaʾkətä, is the plural of mälʾäk, the word the book uses for "angels" (as in "the angels of the presence," 31:14). Used of human leaders it means "chiefs": Charles renders it so, and the site gives mälʾäk the same sense at 10:8, "the chief of the spirits." Charles notes that the Latin omits it. Charles compares the three offices of the Testament of Levi 8, "high priests and judges and scribes."

a: You will be joined to the Lord
t: "Joined to the Lord" or "for the beauty of God"?
p: The Ge'ez plays on Levi's name ("joined"). The Latin has "for the beauty of God."
